title: Raga Sorath
hookLine: the Granth praises Sorath, but only on one condition

cards: A compliment with a condition attached. That's how the Guru Granth Sahib talks about today's raga. Inside the long Var of Sorath, between its stanzas, sits a short salok that names the raga itself.
Sorath, it says, is always lovely. Then comes the word if. Not lovely because of its notes, or its singer, or the hour it's sung.
Lovely if something is true of the person singing it. Today: Raga Sorath, and what the condition is.

teach.h: SORATH FOLLOWS VADHANS IN THE BOOK.
teach.b: The ragas of the Granth come in a fixed order, and this path walks them two days at a time. Sorath follows Vadhans.
Its pages hold hymns by several of the Gurus and by Bhagats whose words the Gurus set beside their own, and then a Var, a ballad of stanzas with saloks between them.
Tradition links Sorath with steady faith; teachers describe raga moods in different ways, so hold that as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. Now the salok.

teach.h: LOVELY IF THE TRUE ONE DWELLS IN THE MIND.
teach.b: In paraphrase: Sorath is always lovely if the true one dwells in the mind. It goes on with plain pictures of a clean mouth and an honest tongue, a person whose speech and heart match. A raga is a mood made of sound.
You could sing Sorath perfectly, every note in place, and by this verse's measure it wouldn't yet be lovely.
The singer finishes the song, with what lives in the mind while the mouth makes music.
And steady faith? A mood that lasts only as long as the song isn't steady. The salok asks for something that stays put when the music stops: the true one held in the mind, always.
Sorath sada suhavani, always lovely, is a big promise for a tune. The verse makes it a promise about a person. Steady faith.

how: In kirtan, ragis sing shabads from the Sorath section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Sorath, and the Var of Sorath, with its saloks between stanzas, is also sung or read in the sangat.

o: the raga after Vadhans, linked with steady faith
the raga of wedding songs and of mourning songs
a closing hymn sung after the evening prayer

games.q: what's inside the raga — tap the pairs.
p: the true one dwells in the mind

s: the Granth praises Sorath with no conditions
the salok says Sorath is always lovely if the true one dwells in the mind.
inside the Var of Sorath, a salok names the raga itself
it praises Sorath, then makes the praise depend on the singer.
every teacher gives each raga the same mood
moods like steady faith come from tradition, and teachers describe them differently.

games.q: you sing Sorath with every note in place. by the salok's measure, is it lovely yet?
o: yes: perfect notes make it lovely.
only if the true one dwells in your mind.
only if it's sung at the right hour.
games.why: the salok puts the beauty in the singer, not the notes: Sorath is always lovely if the true one dwells in the mind.

practice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Sorath; if not, sit in the quiet. Rest on one steady thing, the breath at the tip of the nose or a single word, and when the mind wanders, come back without scolding.
The music can rise and fall around you while the one thing stays; if you pray, let Waheguru be that word, and if you don't, the breath is enough.

wordCard.voice: Raga Sorath. The raga that follows Vadhans, which tradition links with steady faith, and which the Granth calls always lovely, if the true one dwells in the mind. Today's word.
